mcqs.question: A social network graph has 1 million users, each connected to roughly 200 others on average. Why is an adjacency list the right default here rather than an adjacency matrix?
options: The graph is sparse — E is close to V, not V² — so the list's O(V+E) space is far smaller than the matrix's O(V²)
Adjacency lists are always faster for every graph operation regardless of density
An adjacency matrix cannot represent more than a few thousand nodes
Adjacency lists guarantee O(1) edge-existence checks, which matrices cannot provide
mcqs.explanation: With 1 million nodes and roughly 200 edges each, E is around 200 million while V^2 would be a trillion — the list's space scales with actual edges present, while the matrix pays for every possible pair regardless of whether an edge exists. Matrices can technically represent any node count (memory permitting), and it's matrices, not lists, that give O(1) edge checks — the list wins here purely on the sparsity trade-off.

mcqs.question: Kruskal's MST algorithm needs to process all edges in increasing order of weight. Which representation is naturally best suited to this, and why?
options: An adjacency matrix, because edges are already grouped by node
An edge list, because it's already a flat collection of edges ready to be sorted directly
An adjacency list, because it supports O(1) neighbor lookup
None of them — edges must be re-extracted into a separate structure regardless of representation
mcqs.explanation: An edge list is already just a flat collection of (u, v, weight) tuples, so sorting it by weight is a single direct operation with nothing to extract or restructure first. Both the adjacency list and matrix organize information per-node, which is the wrong shape for a global weight-ordering operation and would require flattening into an edge list anyway.

mcqs.question: In an adjacency list, what is the time complexity of enumerating all of a specific node's neighbors?
options: O(V), since every node in the graph must be checked
O(E), since every edge in the graph must be scanned
O(degree), since only the node's own stored neighbor list is touched
O(1), since the neighbor list is precomputed as a single value
mcqs.explanation: An adjacency list stores each node's neighbors directly, so enumerating them only touches that node's own list — proportional to its degree, not the whole graph's size. That's the specific advantage over a matrix, where the same enumeration costs O(V) because the whole row must be scanned even for a low-degree node.

mcqs.question: You're building an undirected graph and need to add an edge between nodes u and v using an adjacency list. What must you do?
options: Append v to graph[u]'s list only, since undirected edges are inferred automatically
Append u to graph[v]'s list only, since direction doesn't matter for undirected edges
Create a new node representing the edge itself
Append v to graph[u]'s list AND append u to graph[v]'s list, since the connection works both ways
mcqs.explanation: An undirected edge means travel is possible in both directions, and an adjacency list has no built-in notion of that — the convention has to be applied manually by mirroring the edge into both endpoints' lists. Adding it to only one side silently produces a graph where traversal from the other endpoint can't reach back, which is a common source of "missing" reachability bugs.

mcqs.question: A problem gives you a 2D grid maze and asks for the shortest path from one cell to another. There's no adjacency list anywhere in the input. What's the right approach?
options: Recognize the grid itself as an implicit graph, generating each cell's neighbors on the fly, and run BFS exactly as you would on any graph
Conclude this isn't a graph problem, since no explicit graph structure is provided
Convert the entire grid into an explicit adjacency matrix before starting any traversal
This problem cannot be solved with standard graph traversal algorithms
mcqs.explanation: A grid is a graph where each cell is a node and adjacent cells (up to 4 or 8 directions) are edges — you compute neighbors on demand instead of materializing a list, and BFS/DFS run completely unchanged on top of that. Converting to an explicit matrix would waste huge amounts of memory for no benefit, and dismissing it as "not a graph problem" misses the entire pattern.

mcqs.question: A graph has 200,000 nodes and roughly 500,000 edges. What's the risk of representing it with an adjacency matrix?
options: There is no risk — matrices always use less memory than adjacency lists
The matrix would need roughly 40 billion cells, which is likely to exceed available memory even though the graph itself is sparse
Adjacency matrices cannot represent graphs with more than 500,000 edges
The matrix would be too slow for edge-existence checks compared to a list
mcqs.explanation: 200,000 squared is 40 billion cells, dwarfing the roughly 500,000 real edges — a stark sparsity mismatch that typically won't fit in memory at all. Matrices are actually faster for O(1) edge-existence checks, not slower, and there's no hard edge-count ceiling on a matrix beyond the memory it demands; the real problem here is defaulting to a matrix without checking density first.
